newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss private bank Pictet eyes Islamic funds.
newsitem.headline: Swiss private bank Pictet eyes Islamic funds.

text.p: Leading Swiss private bank Pictet & Cie is forming an asset management firm with a Kuwait-based Islamic finance company to tap the wealth of Moslems, the first of its kind in Geneva's secretive hub for the rich.

A Pictet bank official said the 50-50 Geneva-based joint venture with The International Investor (TII) will target Islamic clients mainly from wealthy Gulf states and offer Islamic private banking and asset management services.
"We see a demand for Islamic private banking," said Ricardo Payro. "The cake is very large. The market in the Gulf for long-term international investments is growing."

Pictet, managing $62 billion in client funds including assets under custody, has long been offering Islamic banking services to private Arab and Moslem clients in Switzerland, where some $1.8 trillion in private wealth is under management according to recent banking surveys.
But this is the first joint venture of its kind tailored for the Islamic banking market in Geneva, Payro said.

Many Swiss private banks are seeking new niches amidst tough competition in Geneva, where foreign newcomers such as Merrill Lynch and other Wall Street powerhouses have disrupted the once-cosy world of the city's financiers.
Islamic banks and finance institutions, which adhere to the principles of Islamic sharia law, have become popular among the world's more than one billion Moslems.
They do not deal in interest -- the core of the West's banking system -- which is considered by many Moslems as usury and is banned under sharia law.

Payro said Islamic clients, mainly the new generation, were becoming more professional and demanding. Bankers say their private client base is shifting towards younger, fussier and more hands-on investors.

He said the new joint venture will offer asset management services that comply with sharia law and concentrate on global equities -- with a stock selection excluding makers of beer, alcoholic drinks or other products that violate Islamic rules.

Hans Kaufmann, private banking analyst at Bank Julius Baer, said Middle Eastern money represented an important part of Geneva's private banking business following Anglo-Saxon, German and other continental European clients.
But he said Switzerland had recently lost some market share in the Islamic private banking business to other centres in the Far East including Malaysia because of lack of expertise.
"Pictet's entry to this market is a breakthrough. It is not easy for a Swiss private bank to go into a joint venture with an Arab firm. This is a new and difficult world for us," he said.
